cells.tense: The fire and the hours are on the same page, and it shows in what you can do now.
cells.ask: Take one thing you have been rehearsing and use it in front of someone this week — badly is fine.
cells.core:
An idea comes and you stay with it long enough that it turns into something you can do, not just something you felt. The enthusiasm starts a thing, the hours shape it, and the two aren't fighting each other. People feel that sureness in you before they know what you have been working on.

Knowing what your own work is worth without waiting on anyone to confirm it — that's the rare part. The next move is to take one piece of it public. Not polished, not ready by some outside standard. Used once, where someone can see. Something rehearsed alone agrees with you for a long time if it stays in the room.

cells.tense: You're already picturing the finished thing and skipping the part where your hands learn it.
cells.ask: Choose one skill and give it twenty minutes a day for a week, with nothing to show at the end.
cells.core:
You're living a few rooms ahead. The result is already imagined, the reception already rehearsed, and the work you do now keeps getting dragged forward to serve that picture. So nothing gets to be a rough draft. You start things at the level of what they should become, and that's why they don't survive into week two.

What you need is small, slow, and keeps no score. Something you do badly on purpose for a while. One skill for twenty minutes a day this week, unfinished, no audience in your head. Not to get anywhere — to remember what learning with your own hands feels like.

cells.tense: You know what you want to make, and your hands have not been on it in a long while.
cells.ask: Open the piece you set down months ago and work on it for ten minutes — no rebuilding the plan, just touch it.
cells.core:
Some part of you still wants the thing. But it has sat untouched, so each time you think about it, it has become a stranger, and strangers are easy to leave alone. You wait to feel like it before you sit down. That order is backwards.

What brings it back isn't a bright idea, it's a small routine that asks nothing of your mood. Ten minutes on it whether or not you feel like it, tending more than scoring. You have already built a first version of this. Now it needs a little room each day to become real, and that room only gets built by showing up while it is still clumsy.

cells.tense: The work is happening, and you keep describing it as the thing you happen to be doing.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you made recently, however small, and tell someone plainly that you made it.
cells.core:
You put in the hours. Certain things get done with care and repetition, whether or not you feel like it, and if someone asked you to name the last thing you finished, you could. But when you talk about it, the credit goes to the schedule, to having the right tools, to just getting by. Anyone would do it, you say — as though the work didn't come from your own choices.

The choices are already yours. Start telling the truth about one piece of it: that you picked it, you kept at it, you finished it. Not pride. Someone picking up what is already theirs.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the person is already radiating confidence others follow — that is the card's potential, not proof of their history or effect on anyone. The reader could say: my work is private, solitary, nobody follows it; and they would be right, so the cells name the practice itself and the spark kept in it, never an audience. The asks survive being wrong because each one is a small finished move (lay it daily, fix one line, open something a week old) that teaches something about their own practice even if the read misses. The sentence that serves the writer is 'Radiance flows from genuine development' — it flatters the method; in the cells it appears only as the far face, never as a claim about them.
